speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of Labour regarding the dispute in the port of Montreal over the implementation of the Picard report. subtopic: MONTREAL-INQUIRY AS TO FEDERAL INTERVENTION IN DISPUTE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this is a difficult question to deal with, because I cannot accept the premise that the shipping federation has turned down the suggestion made by the minister. When the exchange of useful information has been completed I will make a decision as to whether any intervention is necessary or advisable. speechtext: wish to address a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. speakeroldname: Hon. Robert Winters (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: PROPOSED U.S. QUOTA RESTRICTIONS ON IMPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I saw the report in question and we interpret it differently. At

the bottom of the last paragraph of the report I saw in the press there is reference to a gentleman who said he had been told that 81 senators are backing some form of import quota; the report itself has to do with a growing movement to fight protectionist feelings in the United States. However, I must admit that I do not approve its abolition for one class of the society and its retention for another.
I respect the opinion of those who favour abolition and of those who are opposed to it. I respect the opinion of the member for Rosedale (Mr. D.S. Macdonald) who tries, by respectable means, to sound out the members of the house on that matter. I respect the opinion of the Solicitor General (Mr. Pennell) who advocates the abolition of the death penalty. I respect the opinion of the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Mongrain) who favours its retention.
Personally, I am not ready to reach a decision on that matter, because I feel that we are not mature enough to do so. When we have the means to rehabilitate our prison-ners; when the present government or any other government has passed the legislation which will enable us, for instance, to open

I have a feeling that we are putting the cart before the horse, and that is why I once asked the hon. Solicitor General whether the government should not present its legislation concerning penitentiaries and correctional institutions.
After having discussed the matter with certain persons, I was told that it was almost impossible for the government-and I readily understand why-to introduce legislation in that field before the report of the commission of inquiry, namely the Ouimet commission, had been submitted. I am also told that this commission will be in a position to submit its report in about two or three months at the most.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, this is why yesterday I voted for the adjournment of this debate and this is why today, I intend to bring forward an amendment to this proposal.
I will certainly be in favour of the abolition of capital punishment, Mr. Speaker, when the government is in a position to propose adequate legislation in that field. Now, since the government cannot introduce a piece of legislation in this public sector before that commission has submitted its report, I feel, therefore, that we should have the opportunity to study that report before deciding to abolish capital punishment.
I do not want this debate to become impassioned and emotional; as I said earlier, I respect the opinion of all supporters of retention or abolition. As a matter of fact, I am only concerned with the fate of prisoners capable of rehabilitation, and if I am told that all prisoners are likely to be rehabilitated, well I am especially interested in the lot of the majority of them, since, actually, only a very small number of convicts may be liable to capital punishment, that penalty being meted out at present only to those guilty of premeditated murders.
I say and I repeat that I consider this matter as a free vote. Surely, the house accepts the decision agreed upon by the various political parties of the house, namely that this will be a free vote. I trust no one will accuse anyone, not even the government, in this connection, for having voted for or against capital punishment. This is a free vote. Let everyone decide according to his

Citation 203 (1) of Beauchesne states that it is an imperative rule that every amendment must be relevant to the question under discussion. The law on the relevancy of amendments is that if they are on the same subject matter as the original motion they are admissible, but not when they are foreign thereto.

In my opinion this is a bad bill. Its principle is bad. It abandons all the moral arguments that were put 18 months ago, arguments with which I may not agree but which involve questions of morality and ask the question whether capital punishment is a deterrent. All such considerations have been scrapped by this bill. Certainly it is as immoral to take the life of a murderer who has killed a policeman or security guard as the life of a murderer who in an armed robbery has killed an elderly widow or any other person. The health penalty is kept as a deterrent to prevent the murder of policemen or prison officials. That is the only reason for retaining it in the bill. The death penalty will have a deterrent effect and therefore its inclusion in the bill abuses all logic. That is why this is an entirely bad bill.

Only recently the Minister of Finance was in New York impressing upon his audience at the Economic Club, as I believe it is called, in New York-which is composed of senior executives of a great many financial institutions such as the Chase National Bank and the First City Bank of New York-how greatly Canada requires investment from the United States in order to keep our economic momentum going. Mr. Speaker,
I have been listening very intently, sir, to most of the arguments presented during this debate. Most of the time this house deals with legislative matters respecting finance, transportation, defence and other things, but from time to time we must deal with things that are primarily philosophical in nature, and the bill before us is one which falls into that category.
During this debate we have geared our thinking to what is the new code, and the mores based on our present society. One argument put forward by those in favour of the abolition of capital punishment relates to the sanctity of human life. That is a grand phrase: the sanctity of human life. I realize full well that there are many members in this house who honestly and truly believe in the sanctity of human life. There are untold millions in the world who follow the philosophy that life is sacred. I find it rather strange and difficult to understand some of the proponents of this philosophy who seem to feel that life is only partially sacred. They seem to feel that the taking of the life of a criminal is something that we should not do. At the same time many of these people who argue this point of view support the theory of euthanasia, abortion and other moral theories. If life is sacred it cannot be partially sacred. Sanctity is an absolute term.
What exactly do these people mean when they say life is sacred because of the philosophy of human life and, therefore, we must do away with capital punishment, when at the same time they say in all seriousness that when old people are beyond cure of diseases they may have they should be allowed to die? These people are also those who promote quality population. One cannot be two-sided in this respect. I sometimes wonder if we are being asked to adjust our philosophy to fit this argument. How otherwise are we to accept it?
Obviously life is sacred to the living. If one argues that life is sacred he must also argue 27053-276}
DEBATES	4365
Amendments Respecting Death Sentence that all forms of life should be preserved. This philosophy on the part of those who accept those ideas is difficult to understand. In any event this is a matter for us to consider in so far as capital punishment is concerned. We must decide just exactly what capital punishment is and why it should be imposed. Is it confined to murder or to rape? What manner of things should be considered in relation to the death penalty?
I am not saying that capital punishment should or should not be associated with those things with which it is associated today. Today one's wife does not belong to the husband, nor does one's soul belong to another. It is in terms of our present society that we must decide what justifies punishment of this type. Is capital punishment justifiable in respect of the taking of one's property, as it was at one time? This is no longer the case. Is capital punishment justifiable in respect of the deprivation of property, as it was at one time? This is also no longer the case.
We are faced now with another problem. We no longer possess a complete philosophy which complies with our modern thinking and modern problems. We are still going by the old rules and the old code. Consequently we have a Criminal Code which states that a criminal shall be put to death for having done this or that. We have not examined the situation to find out whether the criminal mores today justify capital punishment.
In reality I do not have too much faith in the argument of sanctity of life. There is a natural abhorrence on the part of the human animal to the killing of its own kind. Hon. members will acknowledge that most species of animal life today do not kill their own species. We have very few animals in the world today which are truly cannibalistic. Man is still an animal species and it is natural that he does not want to kill another of his kind. I have in mind of course a rational man; I am not referring to the irrational man who does commit murder.
Up to this time we have said as a society that we will elect someone to decide, or appoint someone else to deal out the punishment. Killing has always presented a problem. We do not as a species of animal like to kill our own. By and large the human animal does not kill, so long as he is rational and follows his normal instincts. However, those who argue that capital punishment is a deterrent should take note of the fact that it is not a deterrent.
In my many years of practice I have yet to meet one individual who contemplated the
4366	COMMONS
Amendments Respecting Death Sentence punishment that awaited him while committing a criminal offence. These individuals are always convinced they will not be caught. Consequently they do not contemplate the punishment. Indeed, this is the philosophy adopted by soldiers during a war. Not one of them ever imagines there is a bullet for him. They feel that death may come to others, but not to them. This is the natural feeling of the human animal. Therefore capital punishment as a deterrent holds very little weight for the argument in favour of it.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
At the same time I find it very baffling to hear those who support the argument that capital punishment remains a deterrent to the criminal who is incarcerated. If it is not a deterrent, then it is not a deterrent. I shall try later to explain what I think will be the advantage of leaving in the bill that section as it now is. I am inclined to think that capital punishment was never meant to be a deterrent as much as it was meant to be a matter of vengeance. There is a human trait concerned in this aspect of the matter. Man alone, of all creatures on earth, has vengeance and carries vengeance in his heart.
No other creature is a vengeful creature. Vengeance in itself is not to be condemned. It is a human quality. The Lord God was a vengeful God originally. There was originally no limit to vengeance. This is why, when society first began, if one of a neighbouring tribe stole your goods you were not limited to punishing that man in reason; you could at that time kill his whole family, his whole tribe, or do anything. There was no limit to vengeance, until the rise of the Sumerian culture about 4,500 years ago. The Sumerians were the first to place a limit on vengeance. They said: You can take an eye for an eye or a tooth for a tooth. But prior to that, for 2,000 years there was no limit to the vengeance one could exact. The question now is: Have we advanced far enough to say that vengeance shall not be included in capital punishment? It is the relative of the person murdered or the child raped who wants vengeance. He is the one who says: Do you mean to tell me that this murderer will get away scot-free? I want him punished. Therefore vengeance has a great deal to do with what is commonly called deterrence. I believe that vengeance is 90 per cent of the reason for capital punishment and deterrence is about 10 per cent.
Then there is the question of what will happen, after this bill is passed, to those criminals who have been incarcerated. This

DEBATES	November 16, 1967
raises another philosophical question. If you put a man in jail and confine him there for the rest of his natural life, what you have done is make an animal out of a human being. I say this because one of the great instincts of man is that he must have hope and freedom, or at least hope for freedom. We could say that today many of our freedoms do not seem too secure, but there is the hope that they will be. What will happen when we say to a man: Because you have committed murder you are incarcerated for the rest of your life; you will never be released, and if you are never released you are no more than an animal? Indeed, Mr. Speaker, this person will be treated as an animal and will think of himself as an animal. But human nature being what it is, there will always be hope.
I dare say there will be more convictions after the passage of this bill because juries will not be as hesitant to convict a man of murder. As long as juries are composed of 12 men good and true who have to decide on a man's guilt or innocence, in many cases they will have an abhorrence to finding a man guilty if the death sentence is the only result of that verdict. Also, the ultimate sentence could make crown counsel hesitant in his prosecution of a man charged with murder. But once we are sure there will be no capital punishment, juries will be more inclined to find guilty a man charged with murder, and therefore we will have in our jails more prisoners serving life sentences.
However, Mr. Speaker, I do not think you can relate this argument to the fact that you do not have capital punishment. In the United Kingdom more people are now convicted of capital crimes. The fact is that juries have been more inclined to bring in a verdict of guilty. The same thing will happen here.
The argument has been raised as to the possibility of mistake when convicting a man of murder and sentencing him to death. In other words, the argument is that capital punishment should be done away with because of the possibility of mistake. The theory put forward is that our administrative processes could make a mistake and because of this an innocent man could be found guilty. But this is not an argument to be entered into in this debate. It is an argument in support of the very old-fashioned administration of justice. Today we have such sophisticated ideas about telling the truth and testing the validity of statements that it seems we should still trust a jury to decide whether or not a man is guilty, even though it may be
November 16, 1967

influenced by counsel, highly paid or otherwise, in reaching its verdict.
This is a moral argument that the administration of justice needs reform, and I agree 100 per cent. I have discussed this matter with the Solicitor General. I refer to the question of allowing the capital punishment clause to remain in the bill in the event of the murder of a policeman or a person such as a warden performing his duty. Without this provision the abolition of capital punishment will be meaningless. We have not been able to convince our administrators of law and order that we know why criminals act the way they do. They are not sure that we have made any advances in dealing with criminality. They are not sure that this sytem will work and they do not accept the abolition of capital punishment. Without their acceptance you have no law, because if the administrators of law and order do not believe in what the legislators have done, they will find other methods to get their way.
If we consider completely abolishing capital punishment we must consider the reaction of the administrators of law and order. If we incarcerate people and put in their care and control prisoners who could be a threat to the lives of those administering our prison system, in a very short space of time those prisoners would be treated as animals and subjected to such cruelty on the part of our prison administrators as we have never seen before. This is a normal reaction. It has happened before, it has happened in the armed forces. I am sure that many hon. members have examined prison camps of the last war at or just behind the front lines and have found that the treatment afforded prisoners was atrocious. But this is the reaction of prison administrators who do not believe we have found a way of curing the problem of criminality. And we have not. Therefore we have to include this class of people in the bill, to make it workable. The reason I am in favour of the bill-

This clause will not protect them, but it will make them feel more protected.
I know that at the present time we spend little time, energy and research in the whole field of criminology. It was said only a short
DEBATES	4367
Amendments Respecting Death Sentence time ago that we spend more on convicts' shoes than we do in the whole field of research into criminology. This deficit has to be remedied. We are now living in a society that is very complex, and many people cannot adjust to it. We do not know why they turn criminal.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
I recall reading a short time ago about a brother and sister team of doctors in New York who had done 14 or 16 years of research in the field. They have now said they can predict criminal tendencies in a child as early as seven years old. There has been some work started, but we have not done anything in this area. Consequently, if we do have our jails filled, and we are going to have them filled, we will be faced with the problem of what we are going to do in this field of criminology. The only thing we will be able to do will be to spend more time and money in this field, otherwise we will be faced with an insoluble situation.
I should like therefore to support this bill, because when we have this situation we will then be faced with another philosophical problem as to whether we should establish the Devil's Island type of camps, whether we should send these people to Alaska or what we should do with them. I say that what we should do is to spend more time and more money in the whole field of criminology research. For the reasons I have outlined, I wish to support this bill and I hope that it carries.

In this debate, Mr. Speaker, we have all been confronted with the deepest issues in human existence, life, death and society. I do not believe any of us need to apologize, and I do not believe any of us do apologize, for taking the time of this house to debate these fundamental issues. The issues have been argued with sincerity and conviction, and indeed with emotion, in an entirely non-partisan way on both sides of the house.
We have heard statistics used to support the retention of the death penalty in Canada. We have heard statistics used to support the abolition of the death penalty. I have no intention tonight of taking up the time that would be required to examine the statistics for my own argument. Let me say, Mr. Speaker, as others have already said before me, that so far as I am concerned personally I am convinced from the study I have made over a long period of time that capital punishment is not effective enough as a deterrent to murder to justify its retention. In my opinion, its unique deterrent value, its adequate deterrent value, is the only valid reason I can find for retaining the death penalty for any crime. It seems to me that the death penalty stands or falls on that argument, although there are of course other related considerations which affect the issue, some of which I will mention. I think the retentionists as well as the abolitionists accept this position, that the basic question we have to settle is the deterrent value of the capital punishment that some of us wish to abolish.

Many of us believe that capital punishment is in existence for the protection of society, and feel that it should be retained on that basis. The Prime Minister said that three quarters of a loaf was better than none. He also indicated that he hoped the whole matter would soon be disposed of, but it is my understanding that if this bill passes the situation will remain unchanged for five years.

I am very happy to note, Mr. Speaker, that we now identify the hon. member for Gaspe with the Grande Hermine. I rise tonight in consequence of the announcement made by the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Duquet) on November 8 under the authority of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Laing) to the effect that the replica of Jacques Cartier's ship now at La Ronde in Montreal on the Expo site is to be moved to the shipyards in Quebec for protection against ice pressures during the winter.
We are all glad that protection of this kind is to be provided, but I am disturbed by the fact that the hon. member for Quebec East should have been authorized to make the statement he did. It seems the government is now definitely committed to the use of this ship as part of the development of the Car-tier-Brebeuf park in Quebec city.
I know that during the summer the minister had an opportunity to visit the beautiful Gaspe peninsula, where I am sure he was able to admire nature at its best and became convinced that we have not forgotten the historic event which happened there with the landing of Jacques Cartier in 1534. I am sure all hon. members believe this event should be commemorated to a far greater extent than it has. We in the Gaspe believe there is now a wonderful opportunity to restore history and place those events in their proper perspective.
I believe no centennial project has caused more controversy among the people of the province of Quebec than the restoration of the ship Grande Hermine. Incidentally, I am very happy that the minister is here tonight to reply in person. I strongly hope he will reconsider the decision which has been reached because it does seem to me we are embarking on a dangerous course from a historical point of view, one which is likely to cause a distortion of history. The fact that Jacques Cartier landed at Gaspe deserves commemoration in itself. As the minister

heard from the president of our historical society during his visit to Gaspe, there is great danger of our rewriting history and placing Quebec city as the landing place of the great explorer.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
Naturally the reasons given are that we are trying to commemorate the first winter spent by Europeans in this land; but it seems to me much more important that we should commemorate the greatest event, which was the discovery of Canada and the landing at Gaspe in 1534. There is a danger that we are going to distort history. I feel the policy of the government should be determined by the facts of history and be conducted so as to avoid its distortion.
I would like to ask the minister how the government can remain indifferent to the appeal of 3 million people from the province of Quebec, how it can remain indifferent to 505 municipal corporations, 79 boards of trade and 13 historical society groups. All of these have appealed to the government to reverse the decision that has been reached. I hope these appeals will have their effect and that the decision will be reversed.
A further reason for reversing the decision is that we do not yet have the appropriate land in Quebec city to receive the ship. Apparently the city of Quebec has not yet given the land to the federal government. When we think of the enormous expense this development is going to incur, possibly in the neighbourhood of many millions of dollars, then for economic reasons also the decision should be reversed.
The provincial government's policies are those of decentralization and the building up of uneconomic regions. If the government reverses its decision I hope there will flow from it to the Gaspe peninsula and the lower St. Lawrence an opportunity for better development of the tourist industry. Sending the ship to this area would benefit the region. I thank the minister for having stayed in the house tonight, and I do hope he will make some encouraging reply.

maintopic: NORTHERN AFFAIRS-"GRANDE HERMINE"- TRIP TO GASPE FOLLOWING EXPO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on rising I first want to compliment the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Keays) on his persistence in this matter. He has been faithful and continuous in his representation of the aspirations of the people of Gaspe to receive a recognition, which frankly I believe has been overlooked by the people of Canada, and probably by the province

of Quebec. I wish to put on record that I have not seen an area more capable than the Gaspe of attracting visitors in the numbers that I think we should attract from another country, nor have I seen people as competent as the people there to handle the tourist trade and provide the services which tourists want.
I have advised my own people that I want something done in that area, and that we want as much co-operation as we can get from the province of Quebec. To that end the possibility of a national historic park of some dimensions is under very active consideration. I think we have a considerable amount of support from people of influence in the province of Quebec, and I would hope we could make an announcement in respect of that at an early date. I am sure the hon. member knows there is some commemoration there now of Cartier's visit.
I must say to the hon. member that I indicated to the people of Gaspe, when I was there, that we would not be sending the Grande Hermine to Gaspe for the reason that it is not a replica of the ship in which Cartier landed at Gaspe, but a considerably larger ship. We have already removed the Grande Hermine from La Ronde area of Expo, and now it is on its way to Davie Brothers shipyards at Levis in the province of Quebec. We have made arrangements for the ship to be berthed at that site for the winter. It is our further intention that the ship be installed at Cartier-Brebeuf national historic park in the city of Quebec, if the city is able to make the necessary arrangements to expropriate the additional amount of land required for this park.
I should like to advise the hon. member that on my behalf I did authorize the hon. member for Quebec East to make an announcement at Quebec city a week ago. I did this for the specific reason that I thought an announcement of this nature might assist us in the negotiations which are taking place between us and the mayor of Quebec city, and his council, in respect of the acquisition of property there.
I should like to congratulate the hon. member for his persistence in this matter and to assure him that we are giving as much consideration as we possibly can to a nation-, al historic park in Gaspe. Also I should like to assure him that I deeply appreciate the ability of the people there to provide the kind of service he has in mind.
Proceedings on Adjourment Motion

INDIAN AFFAIRS-INABILITY OF INDIANS ON RESERVES TO OBTAIN ADVANCED TRAINING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to see the minister so pleasantly disposed at this late hour. Perhaps he will be as receptive to the matter which I wish to present to him now as he was in respect of the matter raised by the last hon. member.
It is now about three weeks since I asked the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Marchand) whether he was aware that many of the residents of certain Indian reserves across the country are finding it much more difficult, if not impossible, to be accepted into the manpower training programs this year as compared to last year. I had thought that perhaps this was the result of a change in policy or a change in the regulations. I have since found out that there has been no deliberate or specific change in the manpower program policy or in the regulations. It seems, however, that there has been a shift in the application or interpretation of the regulations in respect of the manpower training program.
The shift in application has had the result that many residents of the Indian reserves have not been accepted into the various training programs, which at least theoretically are offered and available to them. I refer specifically to level four of program five which is the basic literacy skills upgrading course. Last year when this course was offered on the Indian reserves with which I am familiar there was a fairly substantial enrolment. I am advised by the chiefs and councillors involved that this year if the basic literacy skills course were offered under the aegis of the manpower branch in one reserve alone, for example Alexander, there would be between 40 and 45 local people who would enrol. Apparently, however, they are not being accepted.
In order to give the minister some indication of my understanding in this regard, my information is that they are not being accepted, not because of any change in policy but rather because of a change in the application of that policy; in other words, because of a change in the interpretation given to it by the regional offices and the officers in the field. I am sure the minister is well aware that Indian people, like any other people, would be much more satisfied if they could avoid welfare payments. In this particular instance it seems that there are only two alternatives. They can be accepted into some of these manpower training programs

If that is not available many of these people will have to revert to welfare. It is true that adult education programs can be of value to these people, and I know that the department of Indian affairs stands ready to offer adult educational courses. However, there is no provision for living allowances. This means that some of these people by taking advantage of the offer, will have to go back on welfare. They might make more of an achievement if they were able to avoid this and enrol in a skill upgrading course, while at the same time earning a living.

speakeroldname: Hon. Arthur Laing (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
maintopic: INDIAN AFFAIRS-INABILITY OF INDIANS ON RESERVES TO OBTAIN ADVANCED TRAINING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want first to thank the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Schreyer) for raising this matter, which has been discussed on a great number of occasions through correspondence from a number of people in Canada, probably because of the manpower regulations. I have been told that in my own area, in the province of British Columbia, for a period of time we were taking in only about one half the number of Indians we took in last year. No doubt the hon. members question relates to the experience at the Fort Alexander reserve, although we have had complaints from other areas in northern Ontario.
We are dealing here with education in respect of this very difficult part of my responsibility, namely the education of Indians. In this field of Indian Affairs I require the support of everyone in the House of Commons, and so far I have received that support, for which I am grateful.
Let me assure the hon. member that in the general field of education we feel we are
doing a very good job at the present time. We now have in federal schools some 32,000 Indians, and 29,000 in non-federal schools, making a total of nearly 62,000. This means an increase from 47,740 to 61,395 in the period 1962 to 1966. There is an increase in enrolment in universities from 131 in 1966 to 240 in 1967. Contrary to the figures presented by the hon. member, we have had an increase in enrolments in vocational schools from 1,234 to over 2,000. There were also some 724 Indians taking upgrading courses in 1966. The budget in 1966 of some $102 million was applied to education to the extent of 50 per cent.
The hon. member has referred to specific problems regarding Fort Alexander Indians. He was concerned about a level four course under the Manitoba system. Because of this situation, in the case of Indians not qualified under manpower, we are prepared to purchase training places for them when they are available. In the meantime, if necessary, we are prepared to set up courses at this level on the reserves, as far as our resources will allow. We will of course purchase wherever possible such courses from the province.
Under the present policy we cannot pay training allowances, as the hon. member pointed out, but students recruited from the unemployed will in most cases, if not in all, be in receipt of welfare at the provincial rates. This does, however, lead to a number of anomalies, such as Indians receiving allowances different from those paid other persons qualifying under manpower. Let me assure the hon. member that we are aware of this situation, and if we can work within the manpower scheme, we intend to do so as quickly as possible. If we cannot, we will find other means of upgrading these courses as far as possible. I thank the hon. member for bringing this matter to our attention.
